notes:
Task and constraints: Return the indices of the two elements of nums that add up to target; exactly one pair exists and an element may not be used twice. n is at most 10^4, so a quadratic scan is affordable.
Idea: Try every pair (i, j) with j > i and return the first pair whose sum equals target.
Technique and why it applies: Plain brute force. With n up to 10^4 it needs at most about 5*10^7 additions, which is the baseline that a hash map improves on.
Invariant: When the outer loop is at i, no pair whose first index is smaller than i sums to target, so the first hit is a valid answer.
Edge cases: Starting j at i + 1 prevents reusing one element; negative values and duplicates such as [3, 3] work because only sums are compared; the final return [] is unreachable under the guarantee.
Complexity: Time is O(n^2) because there are n(n-1)/2 pairs. Extra space is O(1).

Task and constraints: Same Two Sum task; values reach 10^9 in magnitude, so we must look up the exact complement rather than index by value.
Idea: Walk left to right keeping a dictionary from value to its index. For num, check whether target - num is already stored; if yes return both indices, otherwise store num.
Technique and why it applies: A hash map turns the search for the partner into an expected constant-time lookup, removing the inner loop of brute force.
Invariant: Before index i is processed, lookup holds exactly the values at indices below i, so any hit is an earlier, distinct element.
Edge cases: Checking before inserting stops an element from pairing with itself; for [3, 3] and target 6 the second 3 finds the first; negative numbers are fine since the key is the exact complement.
Complexity: Time is O(n) expected because each element costs one lookup and one insert. Space is O(n) for the dictionary.

Task and constraints: Find the length of the longest substring with no repeated character. The string has up to 5*10^4 characters drawn from letters, digits, symbols and spaces, and may be empty.
Idea: Keep the current repeat-free window as a string curr_s. For each character, if it is new append it; otherwise cut curr_s after the earlier copy of that character and append the new one. Track the longest window seen.
Technique and why it applies: This is a sliding window stored as a string. The window never contains duplicates, so its length is bounded by the alphabet size.
Invariant: After each step curr_s is the longest repeat-free substring ending at the current position, and longest_s is the longest one seen so far.
Edge cases: The empty string returns 0; "bbbbb" keeps shrinking the window to one character; the check len(curr_s) >= len(longest_s) is safe because only the length is returned.
Complexity: Time is O(n * sigma), where sigma (about 100) is the alphabet size, because the membership test, index call and slicing each scan a window of at most sigma characters. Space is O(sigma) for the two strings.

Task and constraints: Same longest-substring task, up to 5*10^4 characters, possibly empty.
Idea: Slide a window [left, right]. Store the last index of every character in a dictionary. When s[right] was seen at or after left, move left just past that earlier index. Update the best length after every step.
Technique and why it applies: Sliding window with a last-seen map lets left jump directly instead of moving one step at a time, so each character is processed once.
Invariant: The window s[left..right] has no repeated character after every iteration, and left never moves backwards because of the max.
Edge cases: The max(left, ...) matters when the earlier copy lies before the current window; an empty string leaves the answer at 0; a stale dictionary entry does not break correctness because of that max.
Complexity: Time is O(n), one pass with constant-time dictionary operations. Space is O(sigma) for the dictionary, which is O(1) for a fixed character set.

Task and constraints: Return the median of two sorted arrays with sizes m and n, each at most 1000, with m + n at least 1. The statement asks for logarithmic time; this version is a slower but simple variant.
Idea: Binary search over the value range for the k-th smallest element. For a candidate value num, count how many elements of each array are at most num using a binary search per array; the smallest num with count at least k is the k-th element. The median is that element, or the mean of the two middle ones.
Technique and why it applies: Binary search on the answer, using the sorted order of each array to count in logarithmic time.
Invariant: The search range always contains the k-th smallest value, because the count is monotonic in num.
Edge cases: The range uses only non-empty arrays for its bounds; an empty array contributes a count of 0; an even total averages two k-th values and multiplies by 0.5.
Complexity: Time is O(log(max(m, n)) * log(max_val - min_val)): the outer search halves the value range and each check does binary searches in both arrays. Space is O(1).

Task and constraints: Median of two sorted arrays, sizes up to 1000, total at least 1.
Idea: To find the k-th smallest, binary search on how many elements i come from the shorter array A, so that the rest k - i come from B. The split is right when A[i] >= B[k-1-i]; the k-th element is the larger of the two elements just before the split.
Technique and why it applies: Partition binary search on the shorter array gives the logarithmic bound the statement requires.
Invariant: At every step the first i elements of A and the first k - i of B are candidates for the k smallest, and the search range for i still contains the correct split.
Edge cases: The arrays are swapped so A is the shorter one; out-of-range indices use negative infinity as a sentinel; an even total calls the helper twice and averages.
Complexity: Time is O(log(min(m, n))) per call, since only the shorter array is searched. Space is O(1).

Task and constraints: Return a longest palindromic substring of s, length 1 to 1000, letters and digits only.
Idea: For each index i, first push right past the run of characters equal to s[i], then expand left and right while the two ends match. Keep the longest substring found.
Technique and why it applies: Expand around the center. Skipping the equal run handles even-length palindromes such as "bb" without a second pass.
Invariant: After the expansion for center i, s[left+1:right] is the longest palindrome centered on that run, and res holds the best seen so far.
Edge cases: A single character returns itself; all-equal strings still work but make the run skip long; the bounds check 0 <= left prevents negative indexing.
Complexity: Time is O(n^2) in the worst case, for example a string of one repeated letter, since each center may scan to the ends. Extra space is O(1) besides the returned substring.

Task and constraints: Longest palindromic substring, length up to 1000.
Idea: For every center i, call expand twice, once for odd length (i, i) and once for even length (i, i + 1), and keep the longest result by updating the left and right bounds.
Technique and why it applies: Expansion around centers checks all 2n - 1 possible centers with simple pointer movement, which is enough for n at most 1000.
Invariant: expand returns the length of the longest palindrome around the given center, and left and right always delimit the best palindrome found so far.
Edge cases: An empty result is impossible because n >= 1, but left stays -1 only if no palindrome is longer than the initial value, and then the code returns an empty string; the even call returns 0 when s[i] != s[i+1].
Complexity: Time is O(n^2) because each of the 2n - 1 centers may expand up to n/2 steps. Space is O(1).

Task and constraints: Longest palindromic substring, length up to 1000.
Idea: Manacher's algorithm. Insert a separator between characters so every palindrome has odd length, then compute P[i], the radius at each center, reusing the mirror position inside the rightmost known palindrome. Take the center with the largest radius and map it back to s.
Technique and why it applies: Reusing the mirror radius means the right boundary only moves forward, which gives linear time.
Invariant: center and right describe the palindrome that reaches furthest to the right; for i inside it, P[i] starts at min(right - i, P[mirror]) and is then extended.
Edge cases: The sentinels ^ and $ stop the while loop at the borders; an empty string is handled by preProcess; the start index (max_i - 1 - P[max_i]) // 2 converts back to original indices.
Complexity: Time is O(n) because the extension loop only advances beyond right and right moves at most 2n + 2 positions. Space is O(n) for the transformed string and the array P.

Task and constraints: Write s in a zigzag over numRows rows and read it row by row. Length up to 1000, rows up to 1000.
Idea: Keep a list of row strings. Seed the first numRows characters into their rows, then walk a row index that bounces between the top and bottom rows, appending each next character to its row, and finally join the rows.
Technique and why it applies: Direct simulation of the zigzag; the row index and a direction variable replace any index formula.
Invariant: lines[k] holds the characters of rows k seen so far in reading order, and line_index points to the row that gets the next character.
Edge cases: numRows == 1 and len(s) <= numRows return s unchanged; numRows == 2 uses even and odd slicing; the edge set {0, numRows} triggers the direction flip and the double step when bouncing at the bottom.
Complexity: Time is O(n) with one append per character, assuming CPython's amortized in-place string growth. Space is O(n) for the row strings.

Task and constraints: Zigzag conversion with n up to 1000 and numRows between 1 and 1000.
Idea: Visit rows from top to bottom. A full zigzag cycle has step = 2 * numRows - 2 characters. In row i, take s[j] for j = i, i + step, ...; for middle rows also take the diagonal character at j + step - 2 * i when it exists.
Technique and why it applies: The positions in each row follow an arithmetic pattern, so the answer is built directly without simulating the bounce.
Invariant: Row i is complete after its inner loop, and rows are appended in order, so the output is in reading order.
Edge cases: numRows == 1 returns s because step would be zero; the first and last rows have no diagonal character; the length check j + step - 2 * i < len(s) avoids indexing past the end.
Complexity: Time is O(n) because each character is appended exactly once. Extra space is O(1) besides the output string.

Task and constraints: Reverse the digits of a 32-bit signed integer and return 0 if the result does not fit in [-2^31, 2^31 - 1].
Idea: Remember the sign, take abs(x), reverse its decimal string, convert back to int, restore the sign, then compare against the 32-bit range.
Technique and why it applies: String reversal is the simplest way to reverse digits. Python integers do not overflow, so the range test after reversing is exact.
Invariant: ret always equals the reversed magnitude times the original sign before the final range check.
Edge cases: Trailing zeros vanish after int() (120 becomes 21); -123 becomes -321; a reversal larger than 2^31 - 1 returns 0; the import of bisect is unused.
Complexity: Time is O(d) where d is the number of digits (at most 10 here). Space is O(d) for the digit list and strings.

Task and constraints: Decide whether integer x reads the same forwards and backwards. x is a 32-bit signed integer; the follow-up asks for a solution without converting to a string, which this one does not do.
Idea: Convert x to a string and compare it with its reverse.
Technique and why it applies: A palindrome is by definition equal to its reversal, so slicing with [::-1] decides it in one expression.
Invariant: The string str(x) contains the sign only for negative numbers, so the comparison is exact.
Edge cases: Negative numbers fail automatically because "-121" reversed is "121-"; 0 is a palindrome; numbers with trailing zeros such as 10 fail because the reverse starts with 0.
Complexity: Time is O(d) for d digits. Space is O(d) for the string copies.

Task and constraints: Palindrome Number without converting to a string. x is a 32-bit signed integer.
Idea: Return False for negatives. Otherwise build the reversed number digit by digit using % 10 and // 10 on a copy, then compare it with x.
Technique and why it applies: Arithmetic digit reversal avoids string conversion, and Python integers cannot overflow when the reversed value is built.
Invariant: At each loop step reverse holds the digits already removed from copy in reversed order, and copy holds the remaining prefix.
Edge cases: Negative input returns False at once; 0 skips the loop and reverse stays 0, which equals x; numbers ending in 0 produce a smaller reverse and are rejected.
Complexity: Time is O(log10 x), at most 10 iterations for a 32-bit value, which is O(1) in practice. Space is O(1).

Task and constraints: Match string s against pattern p with '.' (any single character) and '*' (zero or more of the previous element) over the whole string. s has at most 20 characters and p at most 30.
Idea: dp[r][c] says whether the first r characters of s match the first c characters of p. A literal or '.' match copies dp[r-1][c-1]. For '*', either use zero copies (dp[r][c-2]) or one more copy when the previous pattern character matches s[r-1] (dp[r-1][c]).
Technique and why it applies: Two-dimensional dynamic programming on prefixes handles the overlapping choices of how many characters each star consumes.
Invariant: Row r is final once all columns are filled, and every entry depends only on earlier columns of the same row or on row r-1.
Edge cases: dp[0][0] is True; the first row is initialized so patterns like "a*b*" can match the empty string; a star at c = 1 is excluded by the c > 1 guard.
Complexity: Time is O(n * m) for n = len(s) and m = len(p), one constant-time update per cell. Space is O(n * m) for the table.

Task and constraints: Regular expression matching with '.' and '*', len(s) up to 20 and len(p) up to 30.
Idea: result[i][j] is true when the first i characters of s match the first j characters of p. For a non-star pattern character require result[i-1][j-1] and a match; for a star take either result[i][j-2] (zero copies) or result[i-1][j] when s[i-1] matches the starred element.
Technique and why it applies: Bottom-up prefix DP over the two strings, the standard method for wildcard-style matching.
Invariant: Every cell is computed only from cells with smaller i or smaller j, so the table is filled in a valid order.
Edge cases: result[0][j] handles patterns that match the empty string through repeated x*; the guarantee that a star always has a previous character removes the j = 1 case.
Complexity: Time is O(n * m): each of the (n+1)(m+1) cells costs constant time. Space is O(n * m) for the full table.

Task and constraints: Regular expression matching with '.' and '*', len(s) up to 20 and len(p) up to 30.
Idea: Walk both strings with two pointers. When the current pattern element is followed by a star, skip it (zero copies) and push the position on a stack. On a mismatch, pop a saved position and retry by letting the starred element absorb one more character of s.
Technique and why it applies: Iterative backtracking with an explicit stack of choice points, avoiding recursion.
Invariant: Each stack entry records an s position and a pattern position after a star, from which another consumption can be tried.
Edge cases: A trailing run of elements like ".*" is skipped at the end; an empty stack on mismatch returns False; the popped star only expands if its preceding pattern character equals s[last_s_ptr] or is '.'.
Complexity: Time is not established here: the retry loop can revisit similar states and no tight bound is derived, but the small constraints keep it fast. Space is bounded by the number of saved choice points on the stack, which is not tightly bounded here.

Task and constraints: Regular expression matching with '.' and '*', len(s) up to 20 and len(p) up to 30.
Idea: Recursion on the first pattern character. If it is not followed by a star, match one character and recurse on both tails. If it is starred, try skipping the star element, then keep consuming matching characters of s and try the rest after each.
Technique and why it applies: Direct recursive backtracking that mirrors the definition of the pattern, without memoization.
Invariant: isMatch(s, p) is true exactly when the suffix s matches the suffix p, and each call reduces the pair (len(s), len(p)).
Edge cases: Empty p matches only empty s; len(p) == 1 means no star follows; a pattern like ".*" tries every split of s.
Complexity: Time is exponential in the worst case, for example s = "aaaa..." with p = "a*a*a*...b", because the same suffix pairs are solved repeatedly. Space is O(n * (n + m)) in the worst case: recursion depth can reach n + m and each frame holds a copied slice of s.

Task and constraints: Regular expression matching with '.' and '*', len(s) up to 20 and len(p) up to 30.
Idea: The same prefix DP as the full table, but a row only needs the previous row, so keep k = 3 rows and index them with i % k. Reset result[0][0] to False once i > 1 because row 0 is reused for i = 3, 6, and so on.
Technique and why it applies: Rolling-array optimization of the 2D DP, valid because row i reads only row i-1 and itself.
Invariant: Before row i is filled, row (i-1) % k holds the finished values for prefix i - 1 of s.
Edge cases: The start-of-string cell must be cleared after the first row, otherwise stale True values leak in; patterns like "a*" matching the empty string rely on the initialized row 0.
Complexity: Time is O(n * m) as in the full table. Space is O(m) because only 3 rows of length m + 1 are stored.

Task and constraints: Given heights of n vertical lines (2 <= n <= 10^5), find two lines that with the x-axis hold the most water.
Idea: Start with the widest container using the two ends. Compute its area, then move the pointer at the shorter line inward, and keep the maximum area seen.
Technique and why it applies: Two pointers. Moving the taller line can only reduce width without raising the height limit, so only the shorter side can improve the area.
Invariant: Every container that uses an already discarded pointer position is no better than the best area recorded so far.
Edge cases: Equal heights move the left pointer, which is safe; heights of 0 give area 0; n = 2 evaluates a single container.
Complexity: Time is O(n), since each step moves a pointer and they meet after n - 1 steps. Space is O(1).
